transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-06
Start: 15:00 PST
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Luis Ortega (Redwood SE), Riya Patel (Quasar CTO), Marcus Green (Quasar ML Eng), Asha Iyer (Quasar Product), Sam (Quasar intern)

Summary (auto): quick discovery re: model selection for chat + tool-calling, long-context (8k-32k+) needs, multilingual support (EN/ES/JA), hosted vs dedicated vs private tradeoffs, security questions (SOC2, KMS), next steps include pricing, benchmarks, sample data.

Topics: model families (LLaMA, Mistral, MPT, Redwoods-verified), quantization/latency tradeoffs, context window requirements, tool-calling & function call support, multilingual quality, on-prem / VPC options, benchmarks and evals]

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Maya, AE on the account, and with me is Luis, our solutions engineer. How's everyone doing?
[00:12] Riya Patel: Good, thanks. Busy morning but excited to talk through this.
[00:16] Maya Chen: Great. Quick agenda — understand your use cases, context length, where models will run (hosted/dedicated/private), security and compliance, and then outline next steps. Sound good?
[00:28] Marcus Green: Yep. We'll start with the high-level — we build on-device robotics orchestration but run natural language interfaces and planning in the cloud. We need models that can handle long multi-turn plans, up to 10k tokens per session, sometimes stretching toward 25k for whole mission histories. Multilingual is a must — English and Spanish day-to-day, occasional Japanese.
[00:46] Luis Ortega: Okay so long-context is key. Are the 25k sessions single prompt inputs or accumulated across turns?
[00:53] Marcus Green: It's accumulated — we keep full mission logs for audit + retrace. Sometimes we summarize, but often we want the full KV cache available because planning needs the full state.
[01:06] Luis Ortega: Got it. That affects memory and latency. For context like that we'd typically look at models with native long-context support or chunking + KV cache. You mentioned multilingual — what's your quality threshold for Spanish/Japanese? Near-native or acceptable if it's slightly lower?
[01:22] Asha Iyer: Spanish needs to be near-native for our admins, Japanese can be medium quality — just has to understand commands and extract entities.
[01:31] Maya Chen: Quick clarifying Q — do you plan to run in our hosted environment first, or go dedicated/private from day one for data residency?
[01:38] Riya Patel: We prefer hosted for speed, but we have regulatory customers in EU that will eventually require VPC and data residency. So probably hosted to start, then Dedicated reserved capacity for production, and Private for specific enterprise contracts.
[01:51] Maya Chen: That's a common path. Luis, can you walk through model family options and tradeoffs for long context and multilingual?
[01:56] Luis Ortega: Sure. Broadly: LLaMA-derived models (various forks) have good base multilingual capability but you need larger sizes or instruction-tuned variants for quality; Mistral excels in inference efficiency but some variants have shorter native context lengths; MPT/Redwood-verified tuned variants offer better long-context kernels and continuous KV cache optimizations. For 25k we'd evaluate models that support >=32k tokens or use Redwood's chunked-KV approach to stitch contexts — there is a latency cost.
[02:26] Marcus Green: Does Redwood support tool-calling/function calling? We have a planner that needs to call external tools (task planner, simulator) and get structured JSON back.
[02:35] Luis Ortega: Yes — hosted API supports streaming and function/tool calling patterns (we support OpenAI-style function calling and webhook hooks). For Dedicated/Private we can enable the same endpoints; the main difference is network topology and isolation. There are some limits on streaming throughput for large bursts but we can configure burst capacity.
[02:52] Sam: audio glitch, labelled Speaker 4: "can models call our simulator in the loop?"
[02:58] Luis Ortega: They can — tool-calls are synchronous or async; we can set up callbacks to your simulator endpoints inside the VPC for Private deployments, or via secure tunnels for Dedicated. For hosted, we'd recommend putting simulator endpoints behind auth + allowlist.
[03:14] Riya Patel: For latency, our SLAs for some customers are 200–400ms for short planning calls, but for long-run planning we accept 1–3s. How realistic is 200–400ms with 8k+ context?
[03:25] Luis Ortega: Short contexts and smaller models hit 200–400ms; long-context calls at 8k+ usually jump latency to 500ms–1.5s depending on model size and batch. We're aggressive on kernel optimization and prefix-KV caching to keep hot-state latencies low. For strict low-latency SLOs we'd recommend a Dedicated pool with pinned GPUs + quantized model to reduce token latency.
[03:47] Marcus Green: On quantization — any impact on multilingual or tool-calling structured outputs? We worry hallucinations might increase.
[03:55] Luis Ortega: There's some tradeoff. INT8/4 quantization can slightly affect generation fidelity; we have quality profiles for each model family and workload and recommend A/B tests. For structured outputs and tool-calling we usually keep a higher-precision path (FP16) or hybrid quantization for critical routes.
[04:12] Asha Iyer: How do you measure regressions? We need alerting if a rollout hurts Spanish NER or command parsing.
[04:18] Maya Chen: Redwood Optimize ties evals to rollouts — you can attach prompt sets and quality metrics; if the model drifts beyond thresholds we auto-roll back. We'll share a sample eval dashboard.
[04:27] Riya Patel: Good. Can you run benchmarks against our prompts?
[04:30] Luis Ortega: Absolutely. If you share a representative prompt set (we usually ask for 300–1,000 early examples) we'll run latency, token-cost, and quality comparison across 3–4 candidate models and provide a spreadsheet and plots. I'll upload the benchmark plan.
[04:40] Marcus Green: We'll prepare that. On security: SOC2, KMS, SSO/SAML, audit logs are mandatory for us. And EU data residency.
[04:50] Maya Chen: Redwood supports SOC2, SSO/SAML, RBAC, KMS integrations (customer-managed keys on Dedicated/Private), and audit logs with retention tiers. For EU residency we can route workloads to EU regions and for Private you can host the control plane in EU too. We'll share the security brief (link).
[05:04] Riya Patel: Perfect. Any competitors we should be aware of relative strengths?
[05:09] Luis Ortega: Customers frequently compare us to Anthropic for safety controls, OpenAI for model breadth and tool ecosystem, Hugging Face/Replicate for self-host flexibility. We differentiate with unified runtime across hosted/dedicated/private and ops tooling for rollouts and cost controls.
[05:22] Marcus Green: Regarding function calling — does Redwood do typed schema enforcement? We need strict JSON schema validation on tool outputs before ingestion.
[05:31] Luis Ortega: Yes, you can declare schemas for function outputs; we can run validation and either reject, request clarification, or run a secondary extraction step. That's available in both Hosted and Dedicated; Private has the same feature set.
[05:44] Sam (Speaker 4): "who logs the tool calls? is that auditable?"
[05:48] Maya Chen: Tool calls are logged in audit trails, with optional redaction for PII. Logs include timestamps, caller, model variant, and tool payload hashes.
[05:59] Marcus Green: For cost, what's the delta hosted vs dedicated? Ballpark numbers — we have a budget for 1M tokens/month initial.
[06:07] Maya Chen: Hosted per-token pricing is simpler but higher unit cost. Dedicated shifts to commit-based pricing with lower per-token and predictable capacity. For 1M tokens/month we usually see Hosted cheaper on small volumes, Dedicated wins when you exceed sustained usage or need strict latency. I'll send a rough TCO that includes GPU sizing (e.g., gpus for 32k context models).
[06:25] Riya Patel: Any suggestions for model families to shortlist for our workload (long context + multilingual + tool-calls)?
[06:31] Luis Ortega: I'd propose 3 candidates to benchmark: 1) a 32k-tok Redwoods-verified long-context variant (FP16/hybrid), 2) a LLaMA-based instruction-tuned 33B with good Spanish perf, 3) a Mistral-derived efficient model with chunked-KV and aggressive quantization for latency tests. We'll profile latency, cost, and entity-extraction accuracy.
[06:52] Marcus Green: Sounds good. For the 32k option, does Redwood host custom kernels for the attention patterns? We have mission-critical tight loops.
[06:59] Luis Ortega: Yes — our runtime selects optimized kernels and has attention optimizations for long context. For Dedicated we can further tune kernel selection per-customer. On Private, we can ship our runtime package to run in your infra and enable those kernels if hardware supports it.
[07:15] Asha Iyer: Is there a self-serve trial for hosted so our product team can test quickly?
[07:21] Maya Chen: Yes, we offer self-serve with free credits. We'll set you up with an org trial and sample dataset. For benchmarking we'll ask you to use our bench harness though so results are comparable.
[07:30] Riya Patel: Regarding model updates — how do you handle upstream model changes and our pinned versions?
[07:35] Maya Chen: Customers can pin model versions and control rollouts. We keep a model catalog and deprecate with notice; rollouts can be canaryed and tied to evals.
[07:44] Marcus Green: Any gotchas for training/fine-tuning vs instruction tuning? We want to maybe fine-tune for domain-specific robot commands.
[07:51] Luis Ortega: Fine-tuning is possible; we recommend instruction-tuning or adapters for smaller footprint. For Dedicated/Private you can bring your fine-tuned models and we can help with quantization/serving. Fine-tuning might change latency/cost profile so include that in the benchmark plan.
[08:06] Riya Patel: For the multilingual tests, can you run zero-shot Spanish NER and few-shot in-context Spanish tests?
[08:12] Luis Ortega: Yes — we'll include a Spanish NER suite and Japanese command understanding checks. We'll report F1/precision/recall and sample outputs.
[08:20] Maya Chen: Quick note — some of our customers do a hybrid approach: core safety-critical flows run on Dedicated with pinned models, experimental UX in Hosted. That might fit you as well.
[08:31] Asha Iyer: That maps to our roadmap.
[08:33] Riya Patel: Anything else on regulatory or contractual items we should flag?
[08:37] Maya Chen: For EU residency and enterprise contracts we typically require an MSA + DPA; Dedicated has options for customer-managed KMS; Private can be fully air-gapped but has longer provisioning lead time. We'll include contract templates.
[08:52] Marcus Green: About the KV cache and summarization — do you recommend summarizing older history to reduce context size? We prefer keeping raw logs but want cost control.
[09:01] Luis Ortega: Many teams keep hot KV for recent turns and summarize cold history. Redwood supports automatic prefix caching and hierarchical summarization to keep important entities available without sending full history. We can show you cost impact in the bench spreadsheet.
[09:14] Sam (Speaker 4): "any limits on concurrent sessions?"
[09:18] Luis Ortega: For Hosted we limit concurrency per account but can increase with plan; Dedicated you define pool size and autoscaling. We'll size based on your concurrency target.
[09:29] Riya Patel: Ok let's recap.
[09:31] Maya Chen: Recap: we will (1) send hosted vs dedicated pricing/TCO (Maya), (2) Luis will share benchmark plan and upload spreadsheet + suggested test harness, (3) Marcus will share 300–1,000 prompt examples including some 10k+ conversations and multilingual samples, (4) schedule follow-up SE-led deep dive w/ infra and security next week. We'll also share security doc & contract templates.
[09:55] Riya Patel: That works. Any immediate blockers?
[09:58] Maya Chen: Nothing from our side; quick ask — Marcus, if you can include a few mission traces that hit the 20–25k token range that will help kernel profiling.
[10:06] Marcus Green: Will do.
[10:08] Maya Chen: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the links.
[10:12] Asha Iyer: Thanks.
[10:13] Riya Patel: Thanks, bye.
[10:15] End of recording.
